subChunks.title: From Research to Practice: The Evidence-Based Practice Movement and Its Tensions
subChunks.hookHtml: The gap between what research shows and what practitioners do is one of the most stubborn problems in applied psychology and medicine. Studies consistently find that evidence-based interventions take an average of 17 years to move from research publication to routine clinical practice. By then, the evidence may have been revised. Meanwhile, practitioners may be using interventions that evidence has since shown to be ineffective or harmful — or withholding interventions that research supports. The evidence-based practice (EBP) movement emerged in the 1990s, initially in medicine, with the aspiration of ensuring that clinical decisions are informed by the best available research evidence rather than by tradition, authority, or clinical intuition alone. Applied to psychology, EBP involves the integration of best research evidence with clinical expertise and client preferences and values — a formulation that sounds uncontroversial but conceals significant tensions. Who decides what counts as best evidence? What role does clinical expertise play when it conflicts with RCT evidence? How do we apply population-level evidence to individual clients? And what happens when the EBP agenda is captured by cost-driven healthcare systems to justify rationing rather than quality? These are the live debates that every practising psychologist must navigate.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The History and Structure of EBP

Evidence-based medicine (EBM) was articulated by Sackett, Rosenberg, Gray, Haynes, and Richardson (1996) as 'the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients'. The key insight was that clinical experience and intuition, while valuable, are systematically biased and insufficient — clinicians need external evidence from systematic research, especially from RCTs and systematic reviews, to guide decisions that individual patient encounters cannot teach. Applied to psychology, the APA adopted an EBP framework in 2006 that incorporated three components: best available research evidence; clinical expertise; and patient characteristics, culture, and preferences.

The hierarchy of evidence — with systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top, followed by RCTs, then cohort studies, case-control studies, and expert opinion at the bottom — provides a framework for evaluating the quality of evidence. But this hierarchy is frequently misunderstood: it ranks evidence by its ability to establish causal relationships (internal validity), not by clinical relevance (external validity or ecological validity). A well-conducted RCT in a tightly controlled efficacy trial has high internal validity but may have limited applicability to the complex, comorbid patients seen in routine practice.

Efficacy vs. Effectiveness

The distinction between efficacy (does it work under ideal conditions?) and effectiveness (does it work in real-world practice?) is critical for research translation. Efficacy trials typically use: highly selected patients (excluding comorbidity, which is the norm in practice); structured, manualised treatments with adherence checks; specialised research staff; and controlled settings. Effectiveness trials (pragmatic RCTs) and implementation research examine whether the same interventions work in real-world settings with typical patients and clinicians. Effect sizes in effectiveness trials are consistently smaller than in efficacy trials — the 'efficacy-effectiveness gap'. Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations model describes how new practices spread through communities: from innovators and early adopters through the early and late majority to laggards, with multiple barriers at each stage (awareness, acceptability, feasibility, cost, organisational support).

Implementation Science

Implementation science is the study of methods to promote the uptake and integration of evidence-based practices into routine settings. Key frameworks include the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), which identifies five domains affecting implementation: intervention characteristics, outer setting, inner setting (organisational culture), individuals involved, and implementation process. Effective implementation requires attending to: fidelity (is the intervention being delivered as intended?); adaptation (how can it be contextually adapted without losing active ingredients?); and sustainability (how are gains maintained after initial implementation support is withdrawn?).

The Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) cycle (Graham et al.) frames knowledge translation as a cyclical process: knowledge creation (research); distillation (guidelines, summaries); adaptation to context; assessment of barriers; selection of implementation strategies; monitoring knowledge use; and evaluation. This contrasts with the linear 'pipeline' model (research → guideline → practice) that ignores the active process of contextual adaptation required for successful implementation.

Critiques of EBP in Psychology

The EBP agenda in psychology has attracted significant critique. The RCT critique: RCTs measure average treatment effects; individual clients may differ substantially from the trial sample and may not respond as the average does. The 'transdiagnostic' reality of most clinical presentations (multiple co-occurring problems, complex social circumstances) is excluded from most efficacy trials. The manualisation critique: Protocol adherence may reduce the therapist's capacity for responsive, individualised care — 'bending the evidence' to fit the client versus bending the client to fit the evidence. The political critique: EBP guidelines have been used by insurers and health systems to approve only the cheapest evidence-based treatment regardless of individual client needs, effectively using 'evidence-based' as a cost-rationing mechanism. NICE guidelines, while scientifically valuable, specify treatments that may be efficiently delivered at scale — which can marginalise longer-term, relational, or specialist treatments for which efficacy trial evidence is harder to generate.

Clinical expertise and professional judgment: The APA's EBP framework explicitly includes clinical expertise as a component — recognising that experienced clinicians can recognise when standard approaches are inappropriate, integrate information about the individual that no RCT can capture, and provide the responsive, attuned care that the therapeutic relationship requires. The tension is ensuring expertise operates as evidence-informed judgment rather than as a shield against accountability for using ineffective or harmful practices.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen opens with a scenario: 'A client presents with severe depression, social anxiety, a recent bereavement, and a history of childhood trauma. She's also a second-generation immigrant from a culture where psychological therapy is stigmatised. Which RCT does she fit into?' No one answers. 'Exactly. She doesn't fit into any of them. So what does evidence-based practice mean for her?'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Evidence-based practice does not mean 'find the relevant RCT and apply it'. It means using the best available evidence as one input into clinical decision-making, integrated with your clinical expertise and the client's values and circumstances. The APA formulation has three components for a reason. The research tells you what works on average. Clinical expertise tells you how to translate that for this person. Patient values tell you what they actually want and what will engage them.

A student raises the 17-year implementation gap. 'Why does it take so long?' Multiple answers emerge: training doesn't include new methods; organisations don't provide supervision for new approaches; practitioners are already overloaded; guidelines aren't written in accessible language; evidence doesn't reach practitioners through the journals they actually read. Dr. Chen nods. 'Implementation science exists precisely because knowledge production and knowledge use are two different problems.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Be appropriately sceptical when you hear 'evidence-based' used to justify clinical rationing. It's one thing to say 'we prefer treatments with strong evidence because we want to help people effectively'. It's another to say 'we will only fund six sessions of CBT because that's the cheapest evidence-based option' — and apply it regardless of complexity or individual need. The evidence base does not support that policy. That's a cost-control policy dressed in scientific language.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why it's not straightforward to take a research finding about a therapy and apply it directly to individual patients in a clinic.
learningObjectives: Describe the APA's evidence-based practice framework and its three components, distinguishing this from a narrowly research-driven model
Explain the efficacy–effectiveness gap and its implications for research translation, including the relevance of pragmatic RCTs and implementation research
Describe key concepts in implementation science (CFIR, KTA cycle, fidelity and adaptation) and their relevance to closing the research-to-practice gap
Critically evaluate critiques of EBP in psychology, including the RCT critique, manualisation critique, and the political misuse of evidence-based frameworks
commonMistakes: Treating 'evidence-based' as synonymous with 'RCT-tested' — EBP includes multiple evidence types and integrates clinical expertise and patient values alongside research
Ignoring the efficacy-effectiveness gap — applying efficacy trial findings directly to real-world practice without considering the representativeness of the trial sample and setting
Treating clinical expertise as an alternative to research evidence rather than as a complement to it — expertise that operates in the absence of research evidence is not EBP; it is intuition
Conflating NICE guidelines with 'the evidence' — guidelines translate evidence into policy recommendations using explicit value judgments about costs and priorities that are contestable
assessmentCriteria: Demonstrates understanding of the three-component APA EBP model and why each component is necessary
Evaluates the implementation science framework with specific reference to named frameworks (CFIR, KTA) and key concepts (fidelity, adaptation, sustainability)
Shows critical awareness of how 'evidence-based' rhetoric can be deployed to justify cost-rationing rather than quality improvement
Connects EBP debates to clinical realities — the complexity of individual clients, the role of judgment, and the limits of population-level evidence
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A health trust announces that all psychological therapies for depression must be delivered in six sessions or fewer, citing NICE guidelines for 'evidence-based brief CBT'. As a senior psychologist advising on clinical standards, how would you respond to this policy? What evidence would you cite, and what arguments would you make?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
What the evidence actually says: I would first clarify what NICE guidelines actually recommend. NICE (CG90, CG91) does recommend brief CBT (typically 8–16 sessions) for mild-to-moderate depression, and lower-intensity interventions (guided self-help, behavioural activation) for mild depression. However, NICE also recommends: longer-term CBT, IPT, or behavioural couples therapy for more severe depression; psychodynamic therapy for complex presentations; and that clinical judgment should determine the appropriate level of intervention based on individual need, not a blanket session cap. A policy mandating six sessions for all depression presentations therefore misrepresents NICE guidance.

Evidence against a blanket session cap: The evidence does not support a universal six-session limit. Treatment response is variable — some clients achieve remission in six sessions; many do not, and premature termination before response is achieved increases relapse risk. Clients with complex presentations, trauma histories, or significant comorbidity — who constitute a substantial proportion of depression cases in NHS settings — are systematically under-served by brief interventions designed for uncomplicated mild-to-moderate cases. Dose-response studies suggest that outcomes continue to improve with additional sessions up to approximately 24–30 sessions for more complex cases.

What I would recommend: I would advocate for: a stepped-care model with evidence-based session ranges appropriate to each step (low-intensity for mild, moderate for moderate, extended for complex); clinical decision criteria for step-up (insufficient response, complexity indicators, significant risk factors); and genuine clinical flexibility within each step rather than rigid session caps. I would frame this not as opposing EBP but as defending it — the policy as proposed is not evidence-based, it is cost-driven rationing using the language of evidence. Genuine EBP matches intervention intensity to individual clinical need.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: An experienced clinical psychologist argues: 'After twenty years of clinical practice, I've developed a deep knowledge of what works for my clients. Research evidence is useful as background knowledge, but my clinical intuition is a more reliable guide to practice than any RCT.' Critically evaluate this argument (600–800 words), drawing on evidence about clinical judgment, expertise, and the role of research in evidence-based practice.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The argument has a legitimate core but overstates the reliability and superiority of clinical intuition in ways that are not supported by the evidence on clinical judgment. A balanced evaluation must acknowledge what experienced clinicians do well while being honest about the systematic limitations of intuitive clinical judgment.

What experienced clinicians do well: Clinical expertise does provide genuine value that research evidence cannot fully substitute. Experienced clinicians have pattern recognition developed from thousands of clinical encounters — they can recognise atypical presentations, identify when a standard protocol is not fitting, integrate multiple information sources in real time, and attune responsively to the individual in ways that manualised research protocols cannot specify. They also have practitioner knowledge — understanding of what is feasible and acceptable in specific clinical and cultural contexts, and how to adapt interventions accordingly. The APA EBP framework includes clinical expertise as a component precisely because it is irreplaceable.

Where clinical intuition is systematically limited: However, research on clinical judgment consistently finds that it is subject to systematic biases that experience does not correct and may worsen: availability bias (overweighting recent or memorable cases); anchoring (sticking to initial impressions); confirmation bias (seeking information that confirms initial hypotheses); illusory correlation (perceiving relationships between variables that do not statistically exist). Kahneman's System 1 / System 2 framework suggests that intuitive judgments are fast, fluent, and feel accurate — but are generated by the same heuristic-based cognitive system that produces documented errors. Expertise in many domains increases confidence without correspondingly increasing accuracy. Studies of clinical prediction versus actuarial prediction consistently find that statistical prediction (using base rates and structured decision tools) outperforms clinical intuition on average, even when clinicians have access to the same information.

The specific problem with 'what works for my clients': The clinician has no counterfactual — she cannot know whether her clients would have improved equally, more, or less with a different (or no) intervention. Natural recovery, regression to the mean, and the therapeutic alliance common to all bona fide therapies mean that client improvement following any intervention cannot be attributed confidently to that specific intervention without a control condition. Clinical experience simply cannot provide the causal inference that controlled research provides.

The appropriate integration: The most defensible position is not that research replaces clinical judgment but that research provides the external calibration that individual clinical experience cannot self-generate. Experienced clinicians should engage with evidence not as a challenge to their competence but as a tool for improving their judgment — providing base rates for clinical decisions, identifying interventions that work on average and for whom, and flagging when intuitive patterns conflict with research findings. EBP is not research versus expertise — it is research informing and improving expertise. A clinician who insulates herself from research evidence on grounds of twenty years' experience is not demonstrating expertise; she is demonstrating overconfidence.

questions.questionHtml: The APA's 2006 evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) framework identifies three components. Which of the following correctly lists them?
options: RCTs, systematic reviews, and clinical guidelines
Best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient characteristics/culture/preferences
Efficacy evidence, effectiveness evidence, and implementation evidence
Quantitative evidence, qualitative evidence, and mixed-methods evidence
questions.correctAnswer: Best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient characteristics/culture/preferences
questions.explanationHtml: The APA EBPP framework specifies three equal components: (1) best available research evidence — the strongest available research on interventions for the presenting problem; (2) clinical expertise — the practitioner's knowledge, skills, and judgment accumulated through training and experience; and (3) patient characteristics, culture, and preferences — including individual circumstances, values, cultural background, and treatment goals. All three are required; research evidence alone is not EBP.

questions.questionHtml: A CBT intervention for social anxiety shows large effects (d = 1.2) in a university research clinic efficacy trial. When the same intervention is rolled out in NHS Talking Therapies services nationally, average effect sizes are d = 0.5. This difference best illustrates:
options: The publication bias problem in the original trial
The efficacy-effectiveness gap — the difference between outcomes in controlled research conditions and real-world implementation
Treatment drift — therapists deviating from the manualised protocol over time
Regression to the mean in clinical populations
questions.correctAnswer: The efficacy-effectiveness gap — the difference between outcomes in controlled research conditions and real-world implementation
questions.explanationHtml: The efficacy-effectiveness gap describes the consistent finding that effect sizes in efficacy trials (controlled conditions, selected patients, specialised staff) are larger than in effectiveness studies (real-world implementation, typical patients, routine staff). Contributing factors include: typical patients being more complex and comorbid than trial samples; routine therapists having less training and supervision than trial staff; and organisational and contextual factors absent from the trial setting. This does not mean the intervention is ineffective in real-world settings — d = 0.5 is still clinically meaningful — but it illustrates the limits of applying efficacy trial results directly to policy expectations.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: NICE guidelines for psychological therapies are equivalent to the research evidence itself, and clinical practice that deviates from NICE recommendations is therefore not evidence-based.
questions.explanationHtml: False. NICE guidelines translate research evidence into policy recommendations using explicit value judgments about cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and population priorities that are contestable. They represent one authoritative interpretation of the evidence, not the evidence itself. Clinical practice that deviates from NICE guidelines may be justified on the basis of individual clinical need, contraindications, client preferences, or superior local evidence — and may still be evidence-based if it integrates the three APA EBPP components appropriately. Treating guidelines as equivalent to evidence itself mistakes the map for the territory.

The ranking of evidence types by ability to establish causation — from systematic reviews at the top through RCTs, cohort studies, to expert opinion.
The consistent finding that effect sizes in controlled efficacy trials are larger than in real-world effectiveness studies.
A framework identifying five domains affecting implementation: intervention characteristics, outer setting, inner setting, individuals, and implementation process.
